target: AG1’s claim that AI generally makes society better by improving convenience, health, education/work, accessibility, and safety
objection: AI has major harms that outweigh those benefits: it harms the economic well-being of many people and businesses, undermines critical thinking, worsens racism against racial minorities, and creates dangerous privacy risks, so it is not good for society.

target: AG2’s claim that AI harms economic well-being overall
objection: AI can be paired with upskilling, retraining, and productivity gains from automation, so economic outcomes for many people and businesses need not be harmed and may improve instead.

target: AG2’s claim that AI undermines critical thinking in students and adults
objection: AI tutoring can be designed to require explanations, give formative feedback, and correct reasoning rather than just provide answers, so it can strengthen critical thinking instead of weakening it.

target: AG2’s claim that AI worsens racial inequality by repeating and amplifying racism
objection: AI bias can be tested and reduced through data curation, auditing, and other mitigation techniques, so AI does not have to worsen racial inequality for racial minorities.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily creates dangerous privacy harms
objection: AI services can include access controls and privacy-preserving methods, so AI does not have to create dangerous privacy harms.

target: AG1’s broader net-benefit argument that AI is good because it helps in many areas
objection: The claimed harms are substantial enough that AI’s overall net societal effects are negative in practice, even if it also has some benefits.

target: AG2’s claim that AI harms the economy enough to make it bad for society
objection: AI can help detect public-health outbreaks earlier and improve coordination, which reduces disease spread and economic disruption, so AI can improve society’s economic well-being rather than damage it.

target: AG2’s claim that workplace-related AI harms outweigh its value
objection: AI can analyze workplace sensor data to detect hazards and predict maintenance needs, reducing injuries and workplace harm, which is a major societal good.

target: AG2’s claim that AI harms marginalized groups economically or socially
objection: AI accessibility tools such as speech-to-text and real-time captions can help people with disabilities access education and employment, improving the economic well-being of many people and benefiting marginalized groups.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy risks are manageable through ordinary governance
objection: Many AI systems are hard for affected individuals and regulators to interpret or audit because key privacy-relevant details are proprietary or otherwise inaccessible, so privacy violations are difficult to detect, challenge, and remediate.

target: AG2’s claim that AI privacy harms are unavoidable because systems are not readily interpretable or auditable
objection: Existing privacy laws and regulatory frameworks can provide data-subject rights, complaint pathways, investigatory powers, and external oversight, so many AI deployments do have effective transparency and appeal/remedy mechanisms.

target: AG1’s claim that legal rights and external oversight are enough to fix privacy problems
objection: Because AI systems often keep key privacy-relevant information proprietary or inaccessible, affected people often cannot obtain the technical evidence needed to prove a privacy violation, making effective enforcement and remedy unavailable in practice.

target: AG1’s claim that regulators can still enforce privacy rights despite poor transparency
objection: If privacy-relevant model details are inaccessible, people often cannot get enough technical evidence to show a specific AI behavior caused a specific privacy violation, so effective enforcement and remedy are not available in practice.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy harms are effectively unenforceable because victims lack technical evidence
objection: Even when individuals cannot gather technical proof themselves, privacy regulators and courts can investigate, obtain evidence, and order remedies such as corrective orders or compensation, so effective enforcement can still exist.

target: AG1’s claim that regulators can fix privacy harms with corrective action
objection: AI-related privacy harms can persist in learned model parameters and derived artifacts even after deletion or access restriction, so ordinary legal remedies may not effectively stop or reverse the underlying harm at scale.

target: AG2’s claim that AI privacy harms are inherently persistent and poorly remediated
objection: AI can be built with privacy-preserving methods, limited memorization, and model unlearning/retraining so that harmful personal-data influence can be bounded or removed, making privacy harms remediable in practice.
